name: Hydranencephaly
aliases: cystic degeneration of the cerebral hemispheres

reference.source: Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A severe destructive disorder in which the cerebral hemispheres are largely absent and replaced by cerebrospinal-fluid-filled sacs, while the falx, brainstem, and cerebellum are relatively preserved
It is generally a disruption rather than a primary malformation, usually attributed to bilateral internal carotid territory infarction or a destructive insult after the brain has begun to form
The relatively intact brainstem means neonates may initially appear deceptively normal, with preserved brainstem reflexes, sucking, and spontaneous movements
Head size may be normal, small, or progressively enlarged, and transillumination of the skull is characteristically strikingly positive
It must be distinguished from severe hydrocephalus, in which a rim of compressed cortex persists, and from alobar holoprosencephaly, in which midline structures are fused
Later features include developmental failure, irritability, seizures, spasticity, temperature instability, and feeding difficulty
Diagnosis is by imaging, with ultrasound, CT, or MRI showing absent hemispheres, a present falx, and preserved posterior fossa structures
reference.pathophysiology: Hydranencephaly is thought to result from a destructive vascular event, typically bilateral occlusion or infarction in the internal carotid artery territories, occurring after the cerebral hemispheres have begun to develop. The cortex supplied by these vessels undergoes necrosis and resorption, leaving cerebrospinal-fluid-filled sacs bounded by leptomeninges where the hemispheres should be. Because the posterior circulation is spared, the brainstem, cerebellum, and often the thalami and basal structures are relatively preserved, and the falx cerebri, which forms early, usually remains. Other proposed mechanisms include severe intrauterine infection and profound hypoxic-ischaemic injury.
additionalDifferentials: Severe hydrocephalus with a thin preserved cortical mantle
Alobar holoprosencephaly with a monoventricle and fused midline structures
Severe destructive encephalopathy from congenital infection
additionalInvestigations: Brain imaging with ultrasound, CT, or MRI to demonstrate absent hemispheres with a present falx and preserved posterior fossa
Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI when suspected antenatally
Skull transillumination as a supportive bedside finding
Evaluation for congenital infection where the cause is uncertain
redFlags: Progressive macrocephaly with raised intracranial pressure
reference.prognosis: Hydranencephaly carries a very poor prognosis, with most affected infants having profound neurological impairment; many die in infancy, although some survive longer with intensive supportive care. Management is supportive, with shunting sometimes needed for progressive head enlargement.
pitfalls: Being reassured by an apparently normal early neonatal examination because of preserved brainstem function
Mistaking hydranencephaly for severe hydrocephalus and pursuing inappropriate expectations from shunting
Confusing it with alobar holoprosencephaly, which has fused midline structures and an absent falx
Overlooking hypothalamic dysfunction such as temperature instability and endocrine disturbance
management: Care is supportive and palliative, focused on comfort given the profound and irreversible neurological impairment
Ventriculoperitoneal shunting when progressive head enlargement causes discomfort or nursing difficulty
Feeding support with nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding, and management of temperature instability and autonomic dysfunction
Symptomatic relief of spasticity and irritability with attention to positioning and skin care
Multidisciplinary palliative and neurodevelopmental support for the infant and family, including advance care planning
Genetic counselling and evaluation for a recognised cause, with congenital infection assessment where the aetiology is uncertain
